newsitem.title: GERMANY: German spend freeze beckons as job crisis deepens.
newsitem.headline: German spend freeze beckons as job crisis deepens.

text.p: Germany now looks increasingly likely to impose a freeze on all federal government spending as the rising bill associated with its jobless problem endangers entry into European monetary union, economists said on Friday.

The freeze, which government sources had already last month suggested was imminent, will mean any outlay by a government department of more than 500,000 marks ($300,000) will require finance minister Theo Waigel's signature.

"A spending freeze is likely now. Indeed, we're getting used to them," said Joachim Fels, senior economist at Morgan Stanley, adding that such a freeze last year produced savings for Bonn of around five billion marks.
A spokeswoman for the German finance ministry in Bonn said on Friday that no decision had yet been taken on a spending freeze and that she could give no further details.

Germany's Federal Labour Office on Thursday reported a higher-than-expected seasonally-adjusted rise in the number of unemployed workers of 160,000 to 4.317 million in January, some 11.3 percent of the workforce.

As a result, Bonn now faces higher dole costs than it had planned in a budget already tightened to meet EMU requirements, with some estimates reckoning on a further eight billion marks of new costs if joblessness remains around such levels.

Such added costs would push Germany's deficit-to-gross domestic product ratio, which Waigel has forecast at 2.9 percent this year, above the three percent allowed by Maastricht criteria for EMU entry in 1999.

The graveness of the situation was emphasised on Friday as Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher, speaking at a banking congress in Frankfurt, said the jobless crisis was endangering Germany's timely entry into EMU and called on the government to take action.

A rate cut -- the traditional way to stimulate economic growth and in turn create jobs -- was further ruled out by Kuehbacher's Bundesbank council colleague Hans-Joergen Kubnick at the same congress, who said such a move "would not take one unemployed person off the street".

But while Morgan Stanley's Fels said a spending freeze was now increasingly likely, he said it would not in itself be enough to bring Germany's deficit levels below three percent by the end of the year.
"Germany's deficit will end up above three percent of GDP, but that doesn't mean Germany is out of EMU," he said.
Fels said the most likely outcome was now a "soft" EMU in which those countries that were viewed as approaching the Maastricht criteria were allowed to participate.

But other economists said that conflicted with Germany's insistence for a monetary union based on strict adherence to the criteria and that Bonn may yet decide that other measures -- carrying large politicial risks -- were still necessary.

"If Germany wants to continue occupying the moral high-ground on EMU, it may decide that other fiscal measures were required," Midland Global Markets Research senior international economist Ros Lifton said.

Lifton, who also believed a spending freeze was imminent, said Chancellor Helmut Kohl may on top of that decide it needs to increase the contributions currently paid by working Germans for unemployment benefit -- a step carrying clearl political risks.
"But those risks are currently being played down. Kohl's position is not too hot as it stands," she added, noting the deep public resentment of existing austerity measures.
Any ousting of Kohl, whose presence is often held as totemic for currency union, would have potentially far more wide-ranging consequences for the project, including outright postponement, she said.
